newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia says plans review of financial system.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia says plans review of financial system.

text.p: Malaysia's acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim on Friday announced the government was planning to review current regulatory structures in its financial system.

"I have asked the Treasury, Bank Negara and Securities Commission to prepare a review of the current regulatory structures in the financial system and to recommend ways in which these structures can be optimally rationalised," Anwar said in a dinner speech at the Securities Commission (SC) annual dialogue.
Anwar, who is also Finance Minister, said he expects a preliminary report on the review to be completed before the end of the year, after getting industry input.
He said the report was necessary to ensure consistency in the regulation of similar financial products and will promote competition by improving their comparability.
"With the report, we will be in a position to create a more flexible and more responsive regulatory structure...," Anwar said.
Anwar also announced revisions in the SC guidelines for the issue of securities.

For the listing of subsidiary or associated companies of a listed holding company, the threshold level of after-tax profits and/or net tangible assets contribution will be raised to 50 percent from 35 percent.

"With the revision of these quantitative aspects on the chain-listing requirements, which was previously felt to be too restrictive, I hope that more qualified subsidiary or associated companies of listed holding companies will get listed and realise equity capital on their own," the minister said.
Anwar said the planned new exchange for high-growth electronic firms, MESDAQ, may be used to facilitate the secondary trading of fixed-income securities.

"The use of MESDAQ as the trading platform for fixed-income securities is not without precedent. In the U.S., Japan and Germany, secondary trading of bonds is mainly done through over-the-counter markets," Anwar said.
He said the measures were part of the government's efforts to liberalise the country's financial markets.
